title: The princess and the sad dragon
summary: The whole kingdom thinks the dragon on the mountain is furious. Princess Ana is the only one who notices that he's crying.

scenes.text:
Princess Ana was not like the princesses in stories.

She had scraped knees, hair that was never brushed, and a red backpack she never took off. In it she carried bandages, a pair of tweezers, a torch, a jar of honey and a notebook for writing down everything she discovered.

At the castle they said she was a very odd princess. Ana didn't mind. She would rather mend a rabbit's paw than go to a ball.

One night, from the mountains, there came a roar.

So loud that the glasses rattled on the tables and the candles in the dining hall went out.

The next morning, the king stepped out onto the balcony.

"There is a dragon on the mountain," he announced. "Tomorrow at dawn the knights will ride out to find it."

And so the whole kingdom would know, they rang the bells.

That night, the roar came back.

Ana listened from her bed with her eyes wide open. She listened once, and again, and again.

And she noticed something nobody else had.

The roar went up and up, and at the end it broke. It went quieter, with a little hiccup.

Just like when her baby brother cried.

"That dragon isn't angry," she said softly. "He's crying."

Ana got up. She put on her boots, slung on her red backpack and tiptoed down the stairs.

And without a sound, she opened the door.

She climbed the mountain path with her torch lit, while the castle grew smaller and smaller down below.

At the top, among the rocks, there was a huge cave. Out of it came an orange glow, and a warmth that smelled of smoke.

And out of it came the crying.

Ana gulped. She stepped inside.

The dragon filled the whole cave. He had green scales, folded wings, and yellow eyes as big as two cartwheels. And out of those eyes fell tears so fat they made puddles.

When he saw Ana, he went very still.

"I won't hurt you," she said. "I've come to help. What's the matter?"

The dragon hesitated. Then, very slowly, he showed her a paw.

Stuck between two of his claws was an enormous thorn, as long as Ana's arm.

"This is going to hurt for one second," said Ana. "And then it stops. All right?"

The dragon squeezed his eyes shut.

Ana took the tweezers out of her backpack. They were far too small: the thorn was thicker than her thumb. So she put them away, rubbed her hands together the way the blacksmith did, grabbed the thorn with both hands and braced her boots against the dragon's paw.

"On three. One. Two…"

And on two, she pulled.

The thorn came out all at once. Ana landed on her bottom with the thorn in her arms, and a spark escaped from the dragon's nose that scorched the tip of one of her boots.

Ana rubbed honey on the wound and wrapped a white bandage around the claw.

The dragon looked at his paw. He wiggled his claw. And he let out a sigh.

So long and so deep that far below, in the castle, every curtain fluttered at once.

At dawn, the knights marched up the mountain with their lances and their armour, making a tremendous racket.

They reached the cave ready to fight.

And they found Princess Ana asleep, curled up against the dragon's warm tummy, with her red backpack for a pillow. The dragon had a bandage on his paw and his tail curled round her, so she wouldn't get cold.

The dragon opened one eye and looked at them.

The knights didn't know what to do with their lances.

"Shhh," said Ana, without opening her eyes. "He's had a very bad night."

That was how the kingdom met Chispas, who never roared at night again. And ever since, every afternoon, a very odd princess climbs onto his back and the two of them go off to fly.
